title: The Question
text:
Think about the last few movies you watched. How many featured at least two women whose names you knew? Did those women ever speak to each other? And if they did, did they talk about anything other than a man?
These questions form the Bechdel test. A movie passes if:
The Bechdel test is not a complete measure of whether a movie is good, feminist, or free from sexism. A movie can pass while still portraying women poorly, and a movie can fail despite having complex female characters. Instead, the test captures one specific feature of representation: whether women appear as named characters who interact about something beyond a male character.
This simple test leads to a simple curiosity:
How many movies overall pass the Bechdel test?
We cannot watch and classify every movie ever produced so instead, we observe a sample and use it to learn about an unknown population proportion (i.e., the proportion of movies that pass the Bechdel test).

title: The Question
text:
The movie sample
To investigate the proportion of movies that pass the Bechdel test, we will examine a sample of 20 movies. Of these movies:

9 passed the Bechdel test
11 failed the Bechdel test.

The observed pass rate is:
\(9/20 = 0.45\)
In other words, 45% of the movies in this particular sample passed. Our goal is to determine what this result can tell us about \(\pi\), the unknown proportion of comparable movies that pass the test.

title: Sections 6 and 7
text:
The frequentist analysis told us that 9 or fewer passes would not be unusual if \(p\) were 0.50. However, it does not directly answer the question we may be most interested in:

What is the probability that fewer than half of comparable movies pass?

To make a probability statement about \(p\) itself, we need to represent our uncertainty about \(p\) with a probability distribution. This brings us to the Bayesian approach. Unlike the frequentist analysis, Bayesian inference requires us to consider what values of \(p\) seemed plausible before we observed the sample.
Suppose three moviegoers are asked the following question before seeing the sample: What proportion of movies do you believe pass the Bechdel test?

The first expects the pass rate to be relatively low.
The second is genuinely uncertain and does not favor low, middle, or high values.
The third expects the pass rate to be relatively high.

These people do not begin with the same beliefs. A Bayesian analysis does not require us to hide this disagreement. Instead, each person can represent their uncertainty with a prior distribution.
A prior is not simply one predicted value. It is a distribution over all possible values of \(p\). For example, someone might think that \(p\) is probably near 0.30 but admit that values such as 0.20 or 0.50 are also possible. Another person might place equal prior plausibility on every value between 0 and 1.
The prior makes these starting assumptions visible.

title: Sections 3 and 4
text:
Frequentist and Bayesian inference begin with the same data and can use the same Binomial model. Their main difference is how they represent uncertainty about \(p\).


In frequentist inference, \(p\) is fixed but unknown. It does not receive a probability distribution. The sample is random. If we repeatedly selected new samples, the number of passing movies would change. Frequentist methods use this repeated-sampling behavior to evaluate estimators, construct confidence intervals, and perform hypothesis tests.
A frequentist might ask:

Which value of \(p\) makes the observed data most likely?
Which values of \(p\) are reasonably compatible with the sample?
Would 9 or fewer passes be unusual if half of all movies passed?




In Bayesian inference, uncertainty about \(p\) is represented using a probability distribution. The distribution does not mean that the population proportion physically changes at random. Instead, it describes our uncertainty about its fixed but unknown value.
A Bayesian might ask:

Which values of \(p\) seemed plausible before observing these 20 movies?
How should the 9 passes and 11 failures change that uncertainty?
What is the probability that fewer than half of movies pass?

The Bayesian analysis has three main ingredients:
\[
\text{Prior distribution} \times \text{Likelihood} \rightarrow \text{Posterior distribution}
\]

The prior represents uncertainty before the current data.
The likelihood represents the evidence supplied by the current data.
The posterior represents updated uncertainty after combining the two.

title: Sections 10 and 11
text:
Now we reach the central step of Bayesian inference: combining our prior beliefs with the movie data to produce an updated distribution for \(p\).
The general form of Bayes’ rule is:
\[
f(p \mid y) = \frac{f(y \mid p)\, f(p)}{f(y)}
\]
This can be summarized as:
\[
\text{Posterior} \propto \text{Likelihood} \times \text{Prior}
\]
Here:

The prior describes our uncertainty about \(p\) before observing the sample.
The likelihood describes how compatible the observed data are with different values of \(p\).
The posterior describes our updated uncertainty about \(p\) after observing the sample.

The likelihood for the 9 passing and 11 failing movies is:
\[
L(p \mid y) \propto p^{9}(1 - p)^{11}
\]
A Beta prior has the following kernel:
\[
f(p) \propto p^{\alpha - 1}(1 - p)^{\beta - 1}
\]
When we multiply the likelihood and prior, we obtain:
\[
f(p \mid y) \propto p^{9}(1 - p)^{11} \times p^{\alpha - 1}(1 - p)^{\beta - 1}
\]
Combining terms with the same base gives:
\[
f(p \mid y) \propto p^{\alpha + 9 - 1}(1 - p)^{\beta + 11 - 1}
\]
This has the same form as another Beta distribution. Therefore:
\[
p \mid y \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha + 9,\ \beta + 11)
\]
More generally, if \(y\) movies pass out of \(n\) movies:
\[
p \mid y \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha + y,\ \beta + n - y)
\]
The update has a memorable structure:

Posterior \(\alpha\) = prior \(\alpha\) + observed passes
Posterior \(\beta\) = prior \(\beta\) + observed failures

This calculation shows exactly how Bayesian learning occurs. Each observed pass adds to the first parameter, while each observed failure adds to the second. The resulting posterior combines our starting assumptions with the evidence from the sample.


In general, a prior distribution is called conjugate to a likelihood when the resulting posterior belongs to the same family of distributions as the prior. The parameter values change after observing the data, but the type of distribution does not.
In this setting, the Beta distribution is conjugate to the Binomial likelihood. We begin with a Beta prior for \(p\), use a Binomial model for the number of passing movies, and obtain another Beta distribution as the posterior:
\[
\text{Beta prior} + \text{Binomial likelihood} \rightarrow \text{Beta posterior}
\]
For example, if we begin with the uniform prior:
\[
p \sim \text{Beta}(1, 1)
\]
then observing 9 passes and 11 failures produces:
\[
p \mid y \sim \text{Beta}(1 + 9,\ 1 + 11)
\]
\[
p \mid y \sim \text{Beta}(10, 12)
\]
Conjugacy is convenient because it allows us to update the prior by changing only its parameters. Because the posterior remains a Beta distribution, we can easily estimate \(p\), construct credible intervals, and calculate probabilities such as:
\[
P(p < 0.50 \mid \text{data})
\]
Conjugacy is a computational convenience, not evidence that a particular prior is appropriate. We must still explain why the prior is reasonable and examine whether different prior choices meaningfully change our conclusions.

title: Beyond Pass or Fail
text:
This website is intended for students who have completed STAT 360 or a similar probability course and are familiar with frequentist methods. You should be familiar with probability distributions, random variables, expected values, and basic statistical notation.
You do not need previous experience with Bayesian statistics. Concepts such as priors, likelihoods, posterior distributions, conjugacy, credible intervals, and posterior prediction will be introduced from the beginning.
We will briefly review frequentist ideas such as maximum likelihood estimation, confidence intervals, and hypothesis testing. The goal is not to reteach all of frequentist inference, but to use familiar methods as a bridge to Bayesian thinking.

title: Section 1
text:
Let \(p\) represent the unknown proportion of movies in the relevant population that pass the Bechdel test.
\(p = P\)(a randomly selected movie passes the Bechdel test)
If \(p = 0.30\), then approximately 30% of movies in the population pass.
If \(p = 0.50\), then approximately half pass.
If \(p = 0.80\), then approximately 80% pass.
We do not know the true value of \(p\). What we observe is the sample proportion:
\(\hat{p} = y/n\)
Here:
\(\hat{p} = 9/20 = 0.45\)
The sample tells us that 45% of these 20 movies passed. However, \(\hat{p}\) and \(p\) are not the same thing. \(p\) is the unknown population proportion we want to estimate and \(\hat{p}\) is a statistic calculated from the particular sample we observed.
